data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The nocturnal UHI is the delayed release of sensible heat stored during the day in urban thermal mass; the cross-city gap is modulated by sky-view factor, which controls the radiative cooling efficiency of the stored heat.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If measured heat storage change in the urban fabric does not account for the nocturnal energy budget, thermal storage release cannot dominate.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If sky-view factor differences across cities do not correlate with the magnitude of the nocturnal gap after controlling for wind speed, SVF cannot be the single best modulator.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If calm, clear conditions are not maintained, wind-induced sensible heat advection can dominate and obscure the radiative cooling effect.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"By day, impervious low-albedo, high-heat-capacity surfaces (concrete, asphalt) absorb shortwave radiation and sequester it as thermal storage in the building and surface fabric. After sunset, with turbulent sensible heat flux collapsed by the stable boundary layer, longwave radiative exchange and conduction from depth govern cooling. The city cools more slowly because heat conducts back out of storage, maintaining surface and air temperature. The single best cross-city modulator is the sky view factor (SVF): dense, deep street canyons trap outgoing longwave radiation via radiative interchange among facades, sharply reducing net longwave loss to the cold sky. Cities with lower SVF (taller, denser building height) retain more stored heat, producing a larger night-time gap.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
